plan.english: The first man and the twin were brothers. Together they drove the sheep and the cattle into the field, and they found a strewn place under an oak. The oak was old. Then there the man built a hearth. He gave the fire libated honey. The gods spoke to him: "Make the sacrifice." "Seize your dear twin." He heard their word, and his heart trembled. Then he seized the twin and slew him. The twin did not cry out. That was the first sacrifice. He sat down by the hearth, and he did not speak. Then from the twin's flesh the earth came forth. From his head the sky was made. It was broad. Then from his blood the sea arose. And they gave the man good fame. He became the begetter of the people. Then the twin's name became famous.

title: The World from the Twin's Body

plan.english: The twin lay on the strewn place. The gods arrived, and they sat down around him. Then they slit him open. They cut the flesh from the bones. From it they made the earth, and they broke the bones. Then from them they made stones. The blood ran out. Then from it they made the waters. They cut off his head. Then from it they created the sky. From his mind the moon came forth. Then from his tears came the rain-clouds. Then it rained. They set the sun above, and they threw the stars into the night. Then they saw their work. And it was good. They walked on it. They drank the waters, and they became joyful.

Then the man led the twin to the strewn place. The twin looked at the strewn place. He spoke: "I see the fire and the oak." "Where are the sheep? Where are the cattle?" The man said: "You are the sacrifice, brother." Then the twin took fright. He did not flee, and he lay down on the strewn place. Then the man slew him. His heart trembled. His blood ran out onto the strewn place. Then the earth drank it. Then it was getting dark. The stars became bright. Then the man stood there. He did not see his brother.

The man sat down at the hearth, and he cried out. "Brother, where are you?" Then a voice came from below. Then it spoke. "Do not weep." "I am the earth, and I carry you." "I nourish you." "I give you honey and the juice of plants." "I clothe you with wool." "The sky is my head." "The moon is my mind." "The rain-clouds are my tears." "Drink my waters." "Eat my blossoms." "When you die, I cover your bones." "Do not be afraid." "I am your brother." He heard the voice. Then his heart became glad. Then he stood up.

"Whose flesh is the earth?" "The earth is the twin's flesh." "Whose bones are the stones?" "The stones are his bones." "Whose blood is the sea?" "The sea is his blood." "Whose head is the sky?" "The sky is his head." "Whose mind is the moon?" "The moon is his mind." "Who slew the twin?" "The man slew the twin." "What was the first sacrifice?" "The twin was the first sacrifice." "What is left of the twin?" "Imperishable fame is left of him."

The gods sat down at the hearth. The strewn place lay by the oak. Then the man brought the twin to the fire. They laid him on the strewn place, and they gave the fire libated honey. Then they gave it the juice of plants. It burned and cooked the flesh. They, sitting down, ate it and drank the blood. The man stood and looked at the bones. The bones lay in it. It licked the bones. Then from the bones stones arose. They were joyful. They said to him: "You made the first sacrifice." Then the gods stood up. Then it dawned.

The man spoke. "I seized my brother." "I led him into the field." "I slew him." "From him the earth and the sky were made." "My heart trembles." "Where is he?" "That sea yonder is his blood." "This moon is his mind." "I look at the stars." "The stars look at me." "Now I walk." "I eat, I drink." "Brother, do you hear me?" "May you carry me." Then the earth carried him.

Sky saw the slain twin, and he cried out. His tears were great. Then from his tears came the rain-clouds. The sheep were thirsty. Then it rained. The earth drank the water. Then she became full. Then it swelled in the sea. Blossoms arose. Then the snow melted. The sheep ate the blossoms, and they grew strong. Then they drank it. When he cries out, it rains. Then the earth nourishes the flock with it. The men plough the field. They tell this.

The twin spoke to the man. "Seize me, brother, and cut me." "May my flesh become the earth." "May my bones become stones." "May my blood become the sea." "May my head become the sky." "May my name be famous." The man heard the twin's word and wept. His heart trembled. Then he took a stone. Then with it he cut him. From him the earth and the sky came forth. Then the gods set a famous name for the twin. He went away and looked at the stars.

The gods saw the slain twin. They said to him: "Man, do not slay your brother." "Give us cattle." "Let them be the sacrifice." Then they made a pledge with him. Then the man drove them to the fire. They stood there. He gave it libated honey, and he gave it the juice of plants. He said: "Take them." They gave him good things. Then his heart was glad. Now men give cattle to them.

title: The Sons Part Sky and Earth

plan.english: Sky and Earth lay together. The sons dwelt in between. They trembled. Then they grew strong. Then the great son rose. He looked at them and spoke: "Let us lift Sky up." "Let us set her down." Standing, they lifted him up. And they set her down. Then it became bright. Then the mist went away. They caught sight of the sun and became joyful. He stood above, and she lay below. The sun goes in between.

Sky lay on Earth. The men lay under him. They did not stand up. They trembled with fear. Their hearts trembled. A hero had great might. He seized a stone, and he lifted it. Then he struck Sky with it. The stone broke. Then the two split apart. He went up, and she lay down. Then light came in between. They stood up. They caught sight of the sun, and they were glad. Then the hero's name became famous. They tell of the hero's work.

The craftsman stretched the sky above, and he laid the earth below. It was broad. Then in between he set the mist. He threw the stars into the night, and he set the moon above. He yoked swift horses to the wheel of the sun. Then he made the path of the sun straight. Now the wheel of the sun goes through the mist. The horses draw it. Then the sun sinks. Then the craftsman looked at his work. The craftsman sat down. The craftsman's work is great.

The sons cried out. "Father Sky, go up!" "Mother Earth, lie down below!" "We do not see the sun." "We tremble." "We are afraid." He heard, and went up. Then she lay down. The mist went away. Then it became bright. They caught sight of the light, and they became joyful. They spoke again: "Father, giver of good things, stay above!" "Mother, carry us!"

"Where is Sky?" "He is above." "Where is Earth?" "She is below." "What is in between?" "The mist is in between, and the sun goes in between." "Who lifted him up?" "The great son lifted him up." "Whose son was he?" "He was the son of Sky and Earth."

Sky gives water to Earth. She drinks it. Then she nourishes the flock and the sheep. The shepherd drives it into the field. He milks the sheep. From them the wool grows. Men clothe themselves with wool. The dog guards them. The dog is dear to the shepherd. The wolf does not come. Then the wild beasts flee from the dog. "Father, Mother, give us good things." "Give us water and wool." "Let them be many."

The gods hid the fire from the mortals. In winter they grew cold, and they did not cook the flesh. Then a thief arrived. Then having stolen the fire in the gods' hearth, he carried it to the people. The night hid him. Then he ran to them. The thief was swift. The fire burned in their hearths, and they became warm. They became glad. They cooked and ate. The thief's name is famous.

The fire was hidden in the stone. No one knew it. A man sat down by it, and he struck it with a stone. Then the fire ran out. He trembled. Then he became joyful. He put the flesh into the water. It boiled, and it became bright. Then men came to it. They sat down around it. They ate and were sated.

Fire was set in the hearth of the people, and he became their guest. He sat in it. He was red. Then he ate the sacrifice. They gave him honey. They sat there and looked at him. Then fire gave them warmth. He is dear to them. Fire is the master of the dwelling. Fire is their friend. He protects the dwelling. Fire is the giver of good things. Whoever guards Fire, Fire guards him.

title: How the First Man Got Cattle

plan.english: The cattle came forth from below. Then the first man received them. He drove them into the field and milked them. In winter they stood by the oak. They became many, and they grew. The wild beasts fled. Then the wolf arrived. Then the wolf crept toward them. The trusted dog saw the wolf. Then the dog drove the wolf away. The man tamed the dog. The dog was his friend. Then he yoked a team to the yoke. Now the dog sits by the hearth. The shepherd guards them.

The mortals had no king. Then a king was set for them. He was the first king. He made the path straight, and he made a pledge with the clan chiefs. Then he shepherded the free people. He drove the flock inside, and he gave them good things. The clan chiefs heard his words. Then they became many. His might was great. From him the lineage arose. Then his son became king.

The twin was the first king. He was a shepherd of the people. When he was king, no one died. The sheep did not die. The waters did not dry up. The men were not thirsty. Winter did not come. The mortals were many. The men ate and were sated. Then fire burned in their dwellings. The sun shone on them. Then Death came to him. He lay down, and he died. Then the people cried out.

A serpent lay in the fort. It seized the cattle, and it was devouring the sheep. The men trembled. They did not eat. Then a hero came to the fort with swift horses. Then he slew the serpent. He freed them, and he drove them out of the fort. They were glad. Then they ate. The serpent's bones lay in the field. They said: "Hero, you slew the serpent." "Your name is famous."

May the cattle now stand there, may they not flee! May the wolf indeed not come to them! May the snake and the thief not seize them! Dog, guard the sheep and the flock! Shepherd, drive them inside! Now, Sky, give water, Earth, nourish them! May they now be many, may they then grow! May the king have imperishable fame! May the king's flock indeed be great and many!

The twin lay down and did not rise. Then he died. He was the first mortal. No one knew the path. He found it and went along it. The path was long. He did not turn around. Then they followed him. Now he leads the dead along the path. He is the king of the dead. His name is famous. His fame is imperishable.

"Go, dead man, along the path, follow the twin." "Go the way that the twin then went." "Two dogs guard the path." "Indeed, do not be afraid, now enter the boat." "Do not turn around, may dear Fire receive you." "May Earth indeed cover your bones." "May famous Dawn awaken you." "Now may your fame be imperishable."

The mother trembled. She sought her son in the field, and she cried out his name. "My son, where are you?" No voice came. Then she saw an old man. He was sitting by the oak. "Old man, have you seen him?" The old man answered: "I saw him going along the path." "The twin led him." "He is gone." The mother lay down there.

The dead go to the water. They leave the earth. They carry no load. They do not speak. There a boat is standing. The boat is light. The boat swims. They sit down in the boat. The boat transports them. The water is broad. On the other side there is a field. Cattle stand there. The twin sits there, and he is king. He sees the dead coming. He gives them seats.

title: The Sun Returns, the Mortal Does Not

plan.english: The sun sinks and comes again. The moon goes and arrives again. Winter goes and arrives again. The mortal goes and does not come again. Then death comes to him. The dead do not see the sun. His imperishable fame remains. The famous name does not vanish. Whoever has good fame does not die.

The old man died. His wife and his sister cried out, and they laid him on the strewn place. Then they transported him to the fire. It burned the old man's flesh. Then the earth received his bones. They said: "Father, we remember." "May your name remain famous." Then they gave it libated honey. They sat down at the hearth.

A hero saw Death. He said: "Death, where are you going?" Death spoke: "I have come to you." "I seized your father." "Now I am grasping you." The hero said: "Do not seize me!" "Give me imperishable fame." "I am not afraid." Death said: "I seize, I do not give." The hero was silent. Then he went along the path.

When night comes, the mortal lies down. Sleep seizes him. Then he wakes up. Dawn awakens him. No one awakens the dead. The dead do not wake up. The dead lie in the earth. The sun becomes bright, they do not see it. Sleep is the brother of Death.

Father Sky, giver of good things, hear us! You who stand above, you who set the sun up, father, you who gave the day and the light to us. And now Dawn, your daughter, comes. The great son lifted you up. Your rain-clouds fill the sea. Your fame is imperishable. Now hear our word, father! May your light not vanish from us! Give us indeed good fame! Father, now protect us and our flock!

Now, Mother Earth, hear us! You who carry the mortals, you who nourish the flock, you who drink the water of Sky. You are the dear flesh of the slain twin. Mother, you bear the oak and the blossoms. Your fields are broad. Beasts and cattle drink your waters. Give us wool and honey! Mother, may you carry us and the beasts! And when we die, indeed cover our bones.

The wheel of the sun runs through the sky. Swift horses indeed draw it. Swift is the wheel of the sun. Now Dawn dawns, then the sun becomes bright. In the night the sun indeed sinks, and in the day it becomes bright. Now the wheel of the sun does not break. Its path is straight. The sun indeed heats the waters. The dear sun sees us and the beasts. May the sun now see us, may it hear us.

Dear Dawn, daughter of Sky, become bright! You who now awaken the people and the beasts, you who drive the night away. You who indeed bring the swift light of the sun. Now you clothe yourself in a broad garment. When you come, the night grows less. Your light is indeed great. Now come to our hearth, Dawn! Awaken us, Dawn, daughter of Sky!

Now night comes, and day comes. The sun walks in the day. The stars indeed stand in the sky. Winter comes, and the waters grow cold. Then the days grow long. Heat dries the waters. The sun turns, and winter goes. The snow melts; blossoms arise in the field. The sheep indeed grow, and the horses grow. Now who set this in order for the people and the beasts? The gods indeed set this in order for them.

Night, come to the people and the flock! You who cover the earth, you who bring the stars, your stars look at the people. Now the moon walks above. Indeed cover the mortals and the beasts! Sleep comes to us and to the beasts. You are the mother of the stars and of Dawn. Do not frighten our flock, Night! Now may Dawn, daughter of Sky, come to us!

Now, Sky and Earth, hear us! You two are the father and the mother of the gods. The great Sky is stretched above. The broad Earth is indeed stretched below. Now in between stands the mist. In between goes the wheel of the sun. In between it rains; the cattle drink. You two nourish the mortals and the flock. Give us the day and the water, you two!

Then Desire arose first, from Desire the mind arose. Now who stretched the sky? Who laid the earth below? Who indeed made the sea and the oak? Who set the dear sun and the moon above? Now who yoked the swift horses to the wheel of the sun? Who indeed gave the day and the light to the mortals? The gods now know it, and we do not know it. Let us indeed make a sacrifice to them.
